label: 2413lem1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{U}_{n,i}$ and $\mathcal{V}_{n,i}$ denote respectively the subsets of $\mathcal{U}_n$ and $\mathcal{V}_n$ enumerated by $u_{n,i}$ and $v_{n,i}$.  Note that $\mathcal{U}_{n,2}$ and $\mathcal{V}_{n,2}$ are singletons consisting of the sequence $134\cdots n2$, whereas members of $\mathcal{U}_{n,n}$ and $\mathcal{V}_{n,n}$ are synonymous with those in $\mathcal{U}_{n-1}$ and $\mathcal{V}_{n-1}$, which implies the conditions stated for $i=2,n$.  So assume $n \geq 4$, where $3 \leq i \leq n-1$, and we first show \eqref{2413lem1e1}.  To do so, consider whether or not $n$ is the penultimate letter of $\pi \in \mathcal{U}_{n,i}$ with $3 \leq i \leq n-1$.  If so, then $n$ may clearly be deleted yielding $u_{n-1,i}$ possibilities.  If not, then consider the letter $j$ directly succeeding $n$ within $\pi$.  Note $j$ being a descent bottom implies $j \in [2,i-1]$.  Suppose $\pi=\alpha nj\beta i$ (*), where $\beta$ is possibly empty.  Since $j$  is a descent bottom, all letters in $[j-1]$ must occur in $\alpha$.  Further, the set of letters in $[j+1,n-1]$ occurring within $\alpha$ must comprise an interval of the form $[n-m,n-1]$, for otherwise, a 2413 would occur wherein the roles of the `4' and `1' are played by $n$ and $j$.  Note that $i$ occurring to the right of $j$ implies $0 \leq m \leq n-i-1$.  Thus, the sections $\alpha j$ and $j\beta i$ are 2413-avoiding flattened partitions comprising the letters in $[j]\cup[n-m,n-1]$ and $[j,n-m-1]$, respectively.  Upon standardizing, we have $\alpha j \in \mathcal{U}_{j+m,j}$ and $j\beta i \in \mathcal{U}_{n-m-j,i-j+1}$.

Furthermore, we have that all $\pi$ of the form (*), where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are as described above, indeed avoid 2413.  To see this, first note by requiring that $\alpha j$ (and not just $\alpha$ by itself) avoid 2413, we eliminate the possibility of a 2413 arising when the sections $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are combined to form $\pi$ as in (*). If such a 2413 were to arise, the `2' and `1' would be played by letters in $[j-1]$, with the `3' belonging to $[j,n-m-1]$.  Note that indeed any letter in $[j,n-m-1]$ could serve as the `3' due to its lying to the right of $\alpha$, and hence $\alpha j$ avoiding such a 2413 implies $\pi$ does as well.  Moreover, there can clearly be no occurrence of 2413 in $\pi$ of the form (*) with $\alpha,\,\beta$ as stated wherein an element of $[n-m,n-1]$ serves as the `2', as all letters to the right of $n$ are less than $n-m$.  Thus, the conditions stated in the preceding paragraph are both necessary and sufficient for $\pi$ of the form (*) to avoid 2413.  Considering all possible $j$ and $m$ then implies that the double summation expression on the right-hand side of \eqref{2413lem1e1} enumerates all members of $\mathcal{U}_{n,i}$ whose penultimate letter is not $n$.  When taken together with the first case above, one obtains recurrence \eqref{2413lem1e1}.

A similar argument applies to \eqref{2413lem1e2}.  Suppose $\pi \in \mathcal{V}_{n,i}$ whose penultimate letter is not $n$ is decomposed as in (*).  Then all letters in $\beta i$ must now be greater than those in $\alpha$, for otherwise there would be a 3412 wherein the roles of  `4' and `1' are played by $n$ and $j$.  Therefore, the letters in $\beta i$ must comprise $[n-m,n-1]$ for some $m \geq 1$.  Note $j+1 \leq n-m \leq i$ implies $n-i \leq m \leq n-j-1$.  Analogous to before, the requirement that the sections $\alpha j$ and $j\beta i$ both avoid 3412, with $\beta i$ comprising $[n-m,n-1]$ for some $m$ as given, is seen to be both necessary and sufficient for $\pi$ to avoid 3412.  Note that within $j\beta i$, the letter $n-m$ serves as the 2, and hence $i$ acts as $i-(n-m-2)$, in this flattened partition of size $m+1$.  Thus, the sections $\alpha j$ and $j \beta i$ on their respective alphabets are seen to correspond to members of $\mathcal{V}_{n-m-1,j}$ and $\mathcal{V}_{m+1,i-n+m+2}$. Considering all possible $j$ and $m$, and replacing $m$ by $m+n-i$, then accounts for the summation expression in \eqref{2413lem1e2} and completes the proof.

label: 2143lem1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{A}_{n,i}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{n,i}^*$ denote the subsets of $\mathcal{A}_n=\mathcal{P}_n(2143)$ whose members are enumerated by $a_{n,i}$ and $a_{n,i}^*$, respectively.  That $a_{n,2}=a_{n-1}$ is clear, so assume $\pi \in \mathcal{A}_{n,i}$ for some $3 \leq i \leq n$.  Considering the number $j$ of elements in $[i+1,n]$ occurring between $i$ and $2$ within $\pi$ yields \eqref{2143lem1e1}, as deletion of these $j$ elements is seen to result in an arbitrary member of $\mathcal{A}_{n-j,i}^*$ after standardization. Clearly, we have $a_{n,3}^*=1$ and $a_{n,n}^*=a_{n-2}$ for all $n \geq 3$, as $\mathcal{A}_{n,3}^*=\{13245\cdots n\}$ with members of $\mathcal{A}_{n,n}^*$ being synonymous with those in $\mathcal{A}_{n-2}$, upon deletion of the first two letters.

So assume $\pi \in \mathcal{A}_{n,i}^*$, where $4 \leq i \leq n-1$.  We consider cases based on the fourth letter $k$.  If $k=3$, then we may delete $k$ resulting in a member of $\mathcal{A}_{n-1,i-1}^*$.  If $k>i$, then we must have $k=i+1$, for otherwise $i2k(k-1)$ is an occurrence of 2143.  Furthermore, $\pi$ in this case must be of the form $\pi=1i2(i+1)\cdots(i+m)3\pi'$ for some $m \geq 1$, as the members of $[i+1,n]$ must occur in increasing order from left to right within $\pi$.  It is seen that each of the letters in $[i+1,i+m]$ is extraneous concerning the avoidance of 2143 within $\pi$, as is 3.  Deletion of these letters produces an arbitrary member of $\mathcal{A}_{n-m-1,i-1}^*$ for each $m$, and thus considering all possible $m$ yields $\sum_{m=1}^{n-i}a_{n-m-1,i-1}^*$ members of $\mathcal{A}_{n,i}^*$ for which $k=i+1$.  Combining with the prior case where $k=3$ then yields the first summation expression on the right side of \eqref{2143lem1e2}.

Finally, suppose $k \in [4,i-1]$.  In this case, we have $\pi=1i2k\alpha\beta3\pi'$, where $\alpha$ is a possibly empty sequence of letters in $[k+1,i-1]$ in increasing order and $\beta=(i+1)(i+2)\cdots(i+m)$ for some $m \geq0$.  We may delete the letters in $\alpha$ (due to their being preceded by $k$ and $2$) and also those in $\beta$ (due to their comprising an interval starting with $i+1$). Additionally, we have that the $i$ (and hence also 1) may be deleted, for if $i2ab$ is an occurrence of 2143 for some $a>b>i$, then so is $k3ab$.  This leaves the flattened partition $2k3\pi'$, which when standardized is seen to be an arbitrary member of $\mathcal{A}_{n-j-m-2,k-1}^*$, where $j=|\alpha|$.  Considering all possible $k$, $j$ and $m$ then accounts for the second summation in \eqref{2143lem1e2} and completes the proof.

We have
$$A(x,v)=\frac{x(1-\sqrt{1-4x})}{2}-\frac{vx^2(1-3x-(1-x)\sqrt{1-4vx})}{2(1-2x-v(1-x)^2)}$$

label: 2314lem1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{B}_{n,i,j}$ denote the subset of $\mathcal{B}_n$ enumerated by $b_{n,i,j}$ and $\mathcal{B}_{n,j}=\cup_{i=1,i\neq j}^n\mathcal{B}_{n,i,j}$.  If $i>j$, then $\pi \in \mathcal{B}_{n,i,j}$ may be decomposed as $\pi=\pi's\alpha i j$, where $\alpha$ consists of letters in $[j+1,i-1]$ in ascending order and $s \in [j-1]$.  Then we may clearly delete the terminal $j$, due to $i>j$ directly preceding it, as well as the entirety of section $\alpha$, since these letters occur in ascending order and are of intermediate value between $s$ and $i$ (and hence none of them are actually needed in serving as a `1' or `4' in a possible occurrence of 2314). These deletions are seen to result after standardization in a member of $\mathcal{B}_{n-k-1,s,i-k-1}$, where $k=|\alpha|$.  As there are $\binom{i-j-1}{k}$ possibilities for $\alpha$, summing over all $k$ and $s$ yields \eqref{2314l1e1}.  Furthermore, within a member of $\mathcal{B}_{n,i,i+1}$, where $2 \leq i \leq n-1$, the final letter may clearly be deleted, resulting in an arbitrary member of $\mathcal{B}_{n-1,i}$ whose cardinality is given by the right side of \eqref{2314l1e2}.

To show \eqref{2314l1e3}, suppose $\pi \in \mathcal{B}_{n,i,j}$, where $n \geq 4$ and $2 \leq i <j-1 \leq n-1$.  Let $r$ denote the antepenultimate letter of $\pi$ and we consider cases on $r$.   If $r<i$, then we may delete $i$, yielding $\sum_{s=1}^{i-1}b_{n-1,s,j-1}$ possibilities. On the other hand, if $i<r<j$, then we must have $r=i+1$, for if $i+1<r<j$, then $(i+1)rij$ is a 2314.  Since the descent bottoms within a member of $\mathcal{P}_n$ are increasing, the predecessor of $i+1$ must be less than $i$.  In this case, we may delete both $i$ and $i+1$ as they are extraneous concerning the avoidance of 2314.  This leaves a member of $\mathcal{B}_{n-2,s,j-2}$ for some $s \in [i-1]$, and hence there are $\sum_{s=1}^{i-1}b_{n-2,s,j-2}$ possibilities for $\pi$.  The preceding two cases may be combined to give the first summation expression on the right-hand side of \eqref{2314l1e3}.

Now suppose $r \in [j+1,n]$.  Then we have $$\pi=\pi's\delta\beta rij,$$
where $s \in [i-1]$, $\delta$ is either empty or represents the letter $i+1$, and $\beta$ is a possibly empty sequence of letters in $[j+1,r-1]$ in increasing order.  Note that $\delta$ is as described due to $\pi$ ending in $i,j$, with $i<j-1$.  Further, the presence of both $s<i$ and $r>j$ within the increasing run directly preceding $i$ implies that $i$ and $j$ are redundant concerning the avoidance of 2314 (outside of the restriction placed on $\delta$).  Thus, we may delete both $i$ and $j$ and, in turn, all of the letters in $\delta$ and $\beta$ as well. Let $m=|\delta|$ and $k=|\beta|$, and hence $m=0$ or 1 and $0 \leq k \leq r-j-1$, with $\binom{r-j-1}{k}$ possibilities for $\beta$.  Then performing all of these deletions on $\pi$ is seen to result in an arbitrary member of $\mathcal{B}_{n-k-m-2,s,r-k-m-2}$.  Thus, for each $m$, $r$, $k$ and $s$, there are $\binom{r-j-1}{k}b_{n-k-m-2,s,r-k-m-2}$ possibilities for $\pi$.  Considering all possible values of these parameters accounts for the second summation in \eqref{2314l1e3} and completes the proof.

body_md: Formulas \eqref{3214l1e1} and \eqref{3214l1e2} may be justified as \eqref{2314l1e1} and \eqref{2314l1e2} were above, so we focus on \eqref{3214l1e3}.  Let $\mathcal{D}_{n,i,j}$ denote the subset of $\mathcal{D}_n$ enumerated by $d_{n,i,j}$.  Suppose $\pi \in \mathcal{D}_{n,i,j}$, where $2 \leq i<j-1$. Let $s$ denote the rightmost letter of $\pi$ belonging to $[i-1]$ and let $r$ be the antepenultimate letter of $\pi$. If $r \in [i+1,j-1]$, then we must have $r=j-1$ in order to avoid 3214, and hence $\pi$ is expressible as $\pi=\pi's(j-m)(j-m+1)\cdots(j-1)ij$ for some $1 \leq m \leq j-i-1$.  Allowing $m$ to equal zero accounts for the case in which $r<i$.  Note that each of the letters $j-m,\ldots,j-1$ and $i$ may be deleted, leaving a member of $\mathcal{D}_{n-m-1,s,j-m-1}$.  Considering all possible $m$ and $s$ yields the first summation on the right side of \eqref{3214l1e3}.  If $r>j$, then the same argument applies as the one used in justifying the second summation in \eqref{2314l1e3} except that now the number of letters in $[i+1,j-1]$ occurring between $s$ and $i$ may range from 0 to $j-i-1$, with these letters being $j-m,j-m+1,\ldots,j-1$ for each $m$.  Thus, one need only replace $\sum_{m=0}^1$ with $\sum_{m=0}^{j-i-1}$ within the second summation in \eqref{2314l1e3} to account for those members of $\mathcal{D}_{n,i,j}$ wherein $i<j-1$ for which $r>j$.  Combining the prior cases then yields \eqref{3214l1e3} and completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Formula \eqref{4213lem1e1} follows from the definitions, where the extra added one prior to the sum accounts for the no descents permutation $12\cdots n$.  A member $\pi \in \mathcal{E}_{n,i}$ for $3 \leq i \leq n$ is expressible as $\pi=1\alpha i2\beta$, where $\alpha$ consists of elements of a subset of $[2,i-1]$ in increasing order.  Note that this subset must be proper or else $i$ would not be a descent top.  The letters in $\alpha$ are extraneous concerning the avoidance of 4213 as they are followed by $i$ and thus may be deleted, leaving an arbitrary member of $\mathcal{E}_{n-j,i-j}^*$ after standardization, where $j=|\alpha|$.  Considering all possible $0 \leq j \leq i-3$ then implies \eqref{4213lem1e2}.

Deletion of the first two letters of a member of $\mathcal{E}_{n,3}^*$ or $\mathcal{E}_{n,4}^*$ results in a member of $\mathcal{E}_{n-2}$ with no restrictions, whence $e_{n,3}^*=e_{n,4}^*=e_{n-2}$.  Further, $\pi \in \mathcal{E}_{n,n}^*$ implies $\pi=1n\pi'$, where $\pi'$ is $213$-avoiding.  In \cite[Theorem 4]{NR}, it was shown $p_n(213)=2^{n-2}$ for all $n \geq 2$, which implies $e_{n,n}^*=2^{n-4}$ for $n \geq 4$.  Finally, suppose $\pi \in \mathcal{E}_{n,i}^*$, where $n \geq 6$ and $5 \leq i \leq n-1$, and suppose $\pi=1i2x\pi'$, where $x \geq 3$.  We consider several cases on $x$.  If $x=3$, then 3 may clearly be deleted, giving $e_{n-1,i-1}^*$ possibilities.  Now assume $x\in [4,i-1]$. If $x<i-1$, then $x$ must be directly followed by $x+1,x+2,\ldots,i-1$, for otherwise the subsequence $ix3(x+1)$ is an occurrence of 4213.  In particular, if $x \in [4,i-1]$, then $i-1$ must occur somewhere between 2 and 3 within $\pi$.  If 3 directly follows $i-1$, then the letters $x,x+1,\ldots,i-2$ as well as 1 and $i$ may all be deleted, and thus we get $\sum_{m=2}^{i-3}e_{n-m,i-m}^*$ possibilities for $\pi$, upon allowing $x$ to vary.  Combining this with the prior case wherein $x=3$ accounts for the first summation on the right-hand side of \eqref{4213lem1e3}.

So assume either $x\in [i+1,n]$ or $x \in [4,i-1]$, with at least one letter in $[i+1,n]$ occurring prior to 3 in the latter case.  Let $k \in [i+1,n]$ denote the predecessor of 3 in either case.  Then we may write $\pi=1i2\alpha\beta k3\pi'$, where $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\pi'$ are possibly empty and $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are increasing and consist of letters in $[4,i-1]$ and $[i+1,k-1]$, respectively.  Let $m=|\alpha|$ and $j=|\beta|$, where $0 \leq m \leq i-4$ and $0 \leq j \leq k-i-1$.  Then we must have $\alpha=(i-m)(i-m+1)\cdots(i-1)$ in order to avoid 4213, with $\binom{k-i-1}{j}$ possibilities for $\beta$.  Note that all of the letters in $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as well as 1 and $i$ may be deleted, as they place no further restriction on $\pi'$ with regard to 4213 due to $k$ directly following them.  Thus, the subsequence $2k3 \pi'$ is seen to correspond to an arbitrary member of $\mathcal{E}_{n-m-j-2,k-m-j-2}^*$.  Conversely, any $\pi$ of the stated form satisfying all of the requirements given above concerning $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\pi'$ is seen to avoid 4213.  Considering all possible $k$, $j$ and $m$, and replacing $m$ by $m-2$, accounts for the second summation in \eqref{4213lem1e3} and thus completes the proof of \eqref{4213lem1e3}.

Concerning the final statement, we leave it as an exercise for the reader to verify that the same recurrences and initial conditions apply to the arrays $e_{n,i}$ and $e_{n,i}^*$ if they are defined in conjunction with the pattern 4312 instead of 4213.  The argument follows a similar course.  If desired, it is also possible to define a recursive bijection between $\mathcal{E}_n$ and $\mathcal{P}_n(4312)$ drawing upon the various cases used above in proving \eqref{4213lem1e3}.

label: genprop
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{genprop}
Let $\tau$ be a pattern.  Then $p_n(\tau)=p_n(\tau')$ for all $n \geq 1$ if and only if $\tau$ does not start with $1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the sufficiency, suppose $\pi \in \mathcal{P}_n$ contains an occurrence of $	au$ witnessed by the subsequence $xyz$.  Then $	au$ not starting with 1 implies $x 
eq 1$ and hence $1xyz$ is an occurrence of $	au'$.  This implies indeed $\mathcal{P}_n(	au)=\mathcal{P}_n(	au')$, and hence $p_n(	au)=p_n(	au')$, for all $n \geq 1$.

For the necessity, we show that if $	au$ starts with 1, then there exists $n \geq 1$ such that $p_n(	au)
eq p_n(	au')$.  Clearly, we may assume $	au$ has length at least two.  Let $m$ be the smallest $n$ such that $p_n(	au)
eq B_{n-1}$, i.e., there exists a member of $\mathcal{P}_n$ that contains an occurrence of $	au$.  Note that $m$ exists for any pattern $	au$.  We wish to show $p_m(	au')=B_{m-1}$, which would establish the necessity.  Suppose, to the contrary, that $p_m(	au')
eq B_{m-1}$ and let $\pi \in \mathcal{P}_m$ contain an occurrence $s$ of $	au'$.  We may assume that the role of `1' in $s$ is played by the actual letter $1$ and let $x$ denote the letter of $\pi$ playing the role of the `2' in $s$.  First suppose $x$ corresponds to a descent bottom of $\pi$.  Then deletion of the first run of $\pi$ followed by standardization yields a member of $\mathcal{P}_k$ that contains an occurrence of $	au$ for some $k<m$, since the letters of $\pi$ excluding its first run would contain $	au$ in this case.  But then $p_k(	au)
eq B_{k-1}$, which contradicts the minimality of $m$.  So assume $x$ does not correspond to a descent bottom of $\pi$.  Then it is seen that one may delete $x$ in this case and remain a flattened partition as $x$ does not start a run.  The resulting member of $\mathcal{P}_{m-1}$ contains $	au$, as witnessed by the remaining letters of $s$ (the first of which is assumed to be 1).  Again, this contradicts the minimality of $m$, and hence we must have $p_m(	au')=B_{m-1}$, as desired.
